title: Hierarchical Regime-Conditioned Dynamics for Spatiotemporal Graphs
claim: A system can follow distinct latent dynamical modes, and a shared context can branch into different futures depending on the inferred mode.
layout: 2 panels; A is a vertical list of examples, B is a left-to-right timeline that branches at a dashed divider
description: The figure has two panels. Panel A, titled 'System Dynamics', shows three small node-link graphs, each with an arrow pointing to its transformed graph. The arrows are labeled Regime A (Centering), Regime B (Rotation) and Regime C (Square Structure), and they run from pale pink to purple. Panel B is a timeline split by a vertical dashed line into 'Shared Context' on the left and 'Regime-Conditioned Rollout' on the right. On the left, a single curve passes through graph snapshots at t1, t_C/2 and t_C. On the right, the curve splits into three branches, one per regime. The Regime A and C branches are dashed, and the Regime B branch is solid. Each branch ends in graph snapshots at t_C+1 and t_C+H. A legend explains the trajectory line styles and the regime colors, and a time arrow runs along the bottom. The eye goes first to the branching curves.
caption: Example of regime-conditioned graph rollouts. A) The system can evolve according to distinct dynamics referred to as regimes. B) Given an observed graph sequence acting as context, we forecast future node features while inferring the latent regime trajectory that conditions the rollout. The regime exposes which dynamical mode drives the predictions and allows alternative regime-aware futures beyond forecasting alone.
abstract: Forecasting the behavior of spatio-temporal systems often requires more than accurate predictions: models should uncover the dynamical modes governing future evolution. Existing temporal graph and latent dynamical models achieve strong forecasting performance, but their latent representations often entangle multiple dynamical patterns, limiting interpretability. Conversely, regime-inference methods explicitly model such modes but typically do not support generative forecasting over graph-structured systems. We introduce HERON, a self-supervised regime-aware generative framework that unifies graph-structured trajectory generation with regime identification. HERON factorizes the latent state into discrete system-level regimes, capturing global dynamical modes, and continuous entity-level dynamics, yielding a modular regime interface compatible with existing spatio-temporal backbones. Crucially, the inferred regime actively conditions system dynamics, enabling regime tracking and controlled simulations under alternative dynamical modes. Without regime annotations, HERON jointly learns forecasts and regime dynamics in a self-supervised manner, recovering meaningful modes across controlled synthetic and real-world datasets while maintaining competitive forecasting performance. These results open a path toward interpretable, controllable generative modeling of spatio-temporal dynamics.
